newsitem.title: USA: Canadian delays force wheat buyers to look at U.S.
newsitem.headline: Canadian delays force wheat buyers to look at U.S.

text.p: Delayed shipments of Canadian wheat to Pacific ports have forced foreign buyers to look at U.S. white wheat and spring wheat to meet immediate needs, U.S. exporters and traders said.
"It is coming to a head today (Tuesday) because the buyers need the wheat," one U.S. exporter said. "They can't sit around and wait."
The exporter was referring to serious rail shipping delays that have kept more than 1.5 million tonnes of Canadian grain from reaching Canadian Pacific ports since January.
Canadian Wheat Board chief commissioner Lorne Hehn told Reuters earlier Tuesday that 42 vessels were waiting to load on Canada's Pacific Coast on Monday with 13 more ships due by week's end.
"The situation is deteriorating. There's 13 ships due this week. If they all show up we'll be further behind," Hehn said.
The shipping delays forced the CWB to pass up wheat sales for February and March and may now threaten April delivery, Hehn said.
The U.S. exporter added, "They (buyers) are definitely looking at U.S. spring wheat."

"I've seen one Latin American buyer looking to buy 24,000 tonnes U.S. spring for first half March shipment and one African importer looking at 30,000 tonnes U.S. spring wheat for prompt shipment," he said.
Several U.S. exporters and grain merchandisers in the Pacific Northwest said one to two vessels may have been switched to the U.S. from Canada over the past two weeks as a result of the backlog.
"We are hearing this," an Oregon grain merchandiser said. The merchandiser noted trade talk that the vessel switches involved two 30,000 tonne shipments of U.S. spring wheat for prompt shipment.
"There is speculation that some business for U.S. western white wheat might benefit from the delays," another Oregon merchandiser said.

But exporters and analysts stressed that the market had been aware of the delays for several weeks. "This is old news. This has been known for about eight weeks," one U.S. wheat analyst said, who declined to be identifed.

"There have been one or two vessels that have probably been switched from Canada to the U.S. over the past week," he said. "But the quantity has been very small. It's two cargoes and I know it's less than 40,000 tonnes," he said.
"At this point, there is some speculation that Canada may in fact transship grain to ports to the United States, which they have done before," he said.
U.S. wheat futures closed sharply higher on Tuesday, which some traders attributed to improved short-term U.S. wheat export prospects as a result of Canada's shipping problems.
